topic: Sun Tzu: win first, then go to war. 3 laws for walking into meetings already decided, with Klein's pre-mortem

story.title: Sun Tzu drills King Helü's palace women at the court of Wu
story.who: Sun Tzu and King Helü of Wu
story.when: Reign of King Helü of Wu, 514-496 BC (Sima Qian, Shiji 65)

quotes: Thus it is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.
To secure ourselves against defeat lies in our own hands, but the opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple ere the battle is fought.
If words of command are not clear and distinct, if orders are not thoroughly understood, then the general is to blame.

facts.claim: To test Sun Tzu, King Helü of Wu let him drill 180 palace women in two companies. Sun Tzu explained the commands before the drum, the women laughed twice, he had the two company leaders executed, and the next drill was performed with perfect precision
facts.source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) ch. 65, as translated in Lionel Giles, The Art of War (1910), Introduction

facts.claim: Gary Klein's pre-mortem asks a team to imagine a project has already failed and write down why. Klein cites a 1989 study finding that prospective hindsight increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%
facts.source: Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review, September 2007; Mitchell, Russo & Pennington, Back to the Future: Temporal Perspective in the Explanation of Events, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 1989

caption:
Why does the same person win every meeting they walk into?

Around 500 BC, King Helü of Wu handed Sun Tzu 180 palace women and asked him to drill them. Sun Tzu explained every command before the drum sounded. When they laughed, he enforced it. The next drill was flawless. Sima Qian records it in the Shiji.

The Art of War puts it in one line: the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won.

For meeting preparation, that means 3 laws. Make the ask clear before you arrive. Run a pre-mortem, Gary Klein's trick from HBR, the day before. Close your own gaps and let the other side open theirs.

Most people read Sun Tzu Art of War quotes as battle advice. I read them as meeting advice.

Save this before your next big meeting.
